newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Naphtha/Mogas-Mogas up on India, Taiwan buys.
newsitem.headline: Asia Naphtha/Mogas-Mogas up on India, Taiwan buys.

text.p: Talk on light distillates remained thin but prices were supported amid tight supplies and bullish sentiment as India purchased four cargoes for delivery within the first half of March, traders said on Monday.
Traders said the award of 90,000 tonnes of 87-octane unleaded gasoline should extend support for the already tight Asian market.
A source said however that Dutch trader Vitol, the winner of all four cargoes, planned to supply the cargoes from the Mediterranean.
"It does make sense to bring cargoes from the Med," said a trader on the arbitrage window. "But whether you can get physical barrels is another question...the Med has no volume."
A company source said Vitol had won the tender on a combination of prices, at an equivalent of $40 per tonne over Mideast naphtha spot quotes on a cost and freight (c-and-f) basis.

Other sources said the award price was very aggressive at above $1.00 per barrel over Singapore 92-octane unleaded spot quotes, c-and-f. IOC's last gasoline purchase, for February 21-25 delivery to Goa/Kandla, was awarded at $2.50 premium.
Traders in London said on Friday that India had awarded 90,000 tonnes in the tender which closed on February 12 and was valid for two days.

The tender sought three 25,000-tonne cargoes to the west coast--to Bombay and Kandla for March 1-5 and 11-15 delivery, and Goa and Kandla for March 6-10 arrival cost-and-freight (c&f) basis and a fourth for March 1-5 delivery to Madras and Vizag on the Indian east coast.
Talk on Singapore gasoline cargoes was limited to a bid from a Swiss trader at $27.40 per barrel fob, for 50,000 barrels of 92-octane lifting March 4-8.
Traders said it was not surprising that only a bid was heard, ahead of the close of Taiwan's reformate tender for March 16-31 delivery.
Naphtha similarly rose despite lacklustre trading as traders focussed on the Kuwaiti term talks in Singapore which started Monday.
"They just want to hear bids and are not saying anything," said a trader on the talks.
Traders expected bids to be firmer than the last round at $7.90 per tonne over Mideast quotes for August 1996-July 1997 cargoes and the latest conclusion by a Mideast refiner at around $11.00.
"It will go from $12 to $15" a trader said on the possible bids.

Traders said prices are supported as supplies are being held back from the Mideast. Sentiment was also bullish on news on Monday that South Korean refinery Ssangyong will shut down a 200,000 barrel-per-day crude unit for up to five days from February 20.
In the longer term, Singapore supplies were due to fall with the start up of a second petrochemical plant (515,000 tonnes-per-year) in Singapore in April.
Meanwhile regional demand was healthy with an Indian petrochemical company heard seeking 50,000 tonnes for March delivery.
Singapore March swaps rose nearly 25 cents per barrel to $23.85/$24.10, widening the backwardation to April with the forward month largely unchanged at $23.00/$23.30.
(Prices are in dollars per barrel)
